title: Seating Arrangement & Scheduling
shortDescription: Place the strongest clue first and let the rest of the seating chart expose itself — a fixed process beats juggling every clue at once.
genZNote: Place the strongest clue first. Let the rest of the seating chart expose itself — you're not solving a mystery, you're filling in a grid.

sections.heading: Core Idea
sections.body: Seating arrangement and scheduling puzzles give a set of entities (people, events) and a list of clues about their relative positions, then ask for the full arrangement or specific facts about it. Both are solved with the same fixed process: identify the entities, find the FIXED clues, draw a base layout, place the strongest constraints first, resolve what's left, then verify every clue against the finished arrangement.

steps.name: Identify entities and the layout shape
steps.explanation: List every person/event to be placed, and note the shape of the arrangement (straight line, circle facing inward/outward, a table with a fixed number of seats).
steps.purpose: Establishes exactly what needs to be placed and the geometry the clues will refer to.

steps.name: Find the FIXED clues first
steps.explanation: Scan the clues for any that pin an entity to an absolute position ('X sits at one end', 'Y is third from the left') — place these on the diagram before anything relative.
steps.purpose: Fixed clues give you a stable skeleton to build the rest of the arrangement around.

steps.name: Place the strongest relative constraints
steps.explanation: Among the remaining clues, apply the ones that most narrow the possibilities first — e.g. 'immediately to the left of' is stronger than 'somewhere to the left of'.
steps.purpose: Strong constraints eliminate the most possibilities per clue, converging on the answer faster.

steps.name: Resolve remaining positions
steps.explanation: Use the weaker, more general clues to fill in whatever positions are still open, by elimination against what's already placed.
steps.purpose: By this point, most seats should already be constrained enough that only one or two options remain per seat.

steps.name: Verify every clue
steps.explanation: Once the arrangement is complete, re-check it against EVERY given clue, not just the ones used to build it.
steps.purpose: Catches an arrangement that satisfies most clues but silently violates one that wasn't actively used during construction.

sections.heading: Circular Arrangements — Facing Direction Matters
sections.body: For a circular arrangement, always establish whether people are facing INWARD (toward the centre) or OUTWARD (away from the centre) before applying 'left' and 'right' clues — the same physical seat is to a person's left in one facing direction and to their right in the other.

sections.heading: Scheduling — Use a Timeline/Table
sections.body: For scheduling puzzles (who does what on which day/slot), draw a simple timeline or grid with days/slots as columns and entities as rows, and fill it in the same fixed-clues-first order as seating arrangements — the same process applies, just on a linear timeline instead of a seating layout.

sections.heading: Common Traps
bullets: Starting with the vaguest clue instead of the most specific/fixed one, leading to multiple valid-looking arrangements that only get disambiguated much later.
In circular arrangements, applying left/right without first fixing whether everyone faces inward or outward.
Finishing the arrangement without checking it against every original clue — an early-used clue can be silently contradicted later without you noticing.

sections.heading: Exam Strategy
bullets: Always sketch the layout (line, circle, grid) rather than tracking positions purely verbally.
Process clues in order of how much they constrain the arrangement — fixed position clues first, then strong relative clues, then weak ones — not in the order they happen to be written.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Seating and scheduling puzzles are solved by fixing absolute-position clues first, then applying the strongest relative clues, resolving the rest, and verifying against every clue.
keyFacts: Order of attack: entities & layout → fixed clues → strongest relative clues → remaining positions by elimination → full verification.
In circular arrangements, establish inward vs outward facing before applying left/right clues.
Scheduling puzzles use the same process on a timeline/grid instead of a seating layout.
commonConfusion: The same seat is a person's left in one facing direction and their right in the other — facing direction must be settled first.

highYieldFacts: Fixed absolute-position clues should always be placed before any relative clue.
commonTraps: Applying left/right in a circular arrangement before fixing inward/outward facing.
mustRemember: Verify the completed arrangement against every original clue, not just the ones used to build it.
